C. Request of Mayor Davis and Councilmembers Torosis and Zwick that the City Council support the Justice for Renters Act. The California Secretary of State has verified that the Justice for Renters Act has qualified for the November 2024 state ballot. The Justice for Renters Action is an initiative which will expand local control over rent laws by replacing The Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act. Costa Hawkins prohibits rent control on single-family homes, condominiums and rental units that were built after 1995. The Justice for Renters Act removes this ban on rent control in California, giving local communities the right to stabilize rents and make apartments more affordable for low-income and middle-income renters. Repealing Costa Hawkins will help local government address one of the root causes of homelessness--skyrocketing rents and unaffordable housing. Mayor Davis and Councilmembers Torosis and Zwick also request that the City Manager issue a press release indicating the City Council’s support for the proposed ballot initiative and send a letter of support from the City to the Governor, Senator Ben Allen, Assemblymember Rick Zbur, and to the proponents of the Justice For Renters Act.

Staff Report Printout
H. Request of Councilmember Brock that the City Attorney and City Manager consider developing and evaluate the impacts of an ordinance prohibiting the manufacture, sale, and/or installation of engineered countertops in Santa Monica. The fabrication of engineered countertops releases silica dust, and inhalation of silica dust can cause silicosis, a serious and deadly disease. On June 6, 2023, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors adopted a motion instructing the Director of Public Health to report on options to ban the sale, fabrication, and installation of silica fabricated stone in Los Angeles County. In addition, the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health has indicated that they will develop workplace standards for workers who handle engineered stone. Prior to developing a local ordinance, the City Attorney and City Manager are being asked to consider the findings of the Los Angeles County Director of Public health and standards developed by Cal/OSHA to determine its feasibility.   4.E. Conference with Legal Counsel – Considering Whether to

  Whittier, et al. v. Superior Court of Los Angeles County, et al.;
  LASC Case No. 23STCP03579 (requested by Councilmember
  Brock)

  The City Attorney advised the Council approved joining the lawsuit
  by a 4 to 3 vote, with Councilmembers Zwick, Torosis, and Mayor
  Davis voting no.

  Mayor Davis stated her no vote was because she doesn’t think this
  lawsuit will reinstitute cash bail nor will it make the city any safer. It
  simply reverts to the system that we were all existing to prior to
  October 1st, which many people were very concerned about, so she
  does not think this lawsuit in any way makes the city safer, keeps
  more criminals off the streets, and in fact it reduces our ability, the
  county’s ability to come up with a better bail system that the Judicial
  Council is trying to institute.

  Councilmember Torosis stated her no vote was because she has seen
  firsthand how undue incarceration hurts people, hurts families, hurts
  women. And there’s empirical evidence, the Judicial Council of
  California released a recent report finding that a risk-based, zero bail
  system, which is what we have had since the pandemic, has led to
  increased public safety of 5.8% drop in people being re-arrested for
  misdemeanors, a 2.4% decrease of people being re-arrested for
  felonies, and the impact of our pandemic zero-based bail policy
  concluded that the rates of failure to appear in court and re-arrest, or
  new offenses remained either below or similar to historical averages,
  and in fact, for black people, for homeless people, for people with
  severe mental illnesses, the failure to appear rate was actually lower
  than it was prior to these zero-based policies. She also thinks it
  criminalizes poverty and perpetuates inequality in justice in our
  criminal legal system, and that’s actually why our courts have ordered

  3  October 10, 2023

  that cash bail is unconstitutional. It doesn’t prevent crime from
  happening, but it keeps low-income individuals and disproportionally
  people of color in jail before trial. Black folks are much more likely

  people, and we all here believe in innocent until proven guilty. We
  are not talking about release after trial, we’re talking about pre-
  arraignment procedures. We should give L.A. Superior Court time to
  implement these procedures before spending county resources on ill-
  fated lawsuit that is likely going to be dismissed.

  STUDY SESSION:  7.A. Discussion on the Lottery-Selected Panel Process for the
  AIRPORT PANEL PROCESS  Airport, was presented.

  Recommended Action
  Staff recommends that City Council:
  1. Review and comment on the democratic lottery process as the
  primary public engagement method for the Future of the Santa
  Monica Airport project;
  2. Provide direction to staff about: the framing question the
  Lottery Selected Panel would answer and whether the Lottery
  Selected Panel should be comprised of Santa Monica residents
  only or also include business owners and/or people from the
  adjacent West Los Angeles area; and
  3. Direct staff to prepare a sole source contract, as an exception
  to the competitive bidding process pursuant to Section
  2.24.250 (b), for Healthy Democracy to provide the services
  related to the democratic lottery process and bring it back for
  Council review in November.

  Questions asked and answered of staff included: this is not the only
  opportunity for people to weigh in on the Future of the Airport
  process; does the Council have to accept the recommendation; are the
  panels open to the public; isn’t there an information committee that is
  being formed, and will board and commission be involved in the

  information committee; how do we ensure that we have a statistically
  diverse demographic on the committee; what exactly defines
  demographic; what information is being included in the letter being
  sent out to potential committee members; what is meant by “balanced
  information”; why was any mention of a park or Measure LC in the
  staff report or any of the documents; whose going to be administering
  the third party evaluation process; whose being called in as
  professionals as part of the evaluation process; is there a relationship
  between Healthy Democracy and former Housing Commissioner
  Leonora Camner; what is the cost of the Healthy Democracy process;
  why wasn’t a RFP done and where do the other firms fall that weren’t
  recommended; what is the end result in Petaluma; what are the
  international projects and where are they; how do we get more
  information on the specificity of what the lottery system is going to
  be in order to reassure the public that the wishes of Measure LC will
  be upheld; if we went through a normal process, how would that look
  compared to the recommended lottery process; how much staff time
  would it take to do this process in-house as opposed to going with an
  outside consultant, and what would that look like; who will have the
  ultimate authority on making the final decision on the
  recommendation; what about Measure LC, will it have to change or
  be rewritten to meet the recommendation; what are the traditional
  failures in the process the way things are; how does this process make
  the conversation less confrontational; what are the stakeholders
  opportunities to participate in the information process; how does the
  random selection process work; if people are selected, how do you
  mitigate the different levels of education, socio-economic status to
  ensure that everybody’s starting at the same point; how do you deal
  with the activist voice at the table, and how can they be heard; is there
  any time when a process has not gone well; how do we create a
  process that brings more people into the process; did our staff reach
  out to Petaluma to find out their satisfaction with the lottery process;
  with regards to Healthy Democracy, is there anything they do to
  guide the results; is one of the benefits that staff sees is that the
  recommendation was a rigorous process that has legitimacy to it
  that’s hard to ignore; how long would a complete RFP process for the
  public participation take; are there other groups who do the same type
  of work as Healthy Democracy; why are we still at only one vendor,
  and was there a wider net cast in the RFQ process; what are the past
  processes for outreach; and, what is the ability of any other group to
  ensure a broader input from the public.

  Considerable discussion ensued on topics including, but not limited
  to: there doesn’t seem like Healthy Democracy has a lot of projects
  that they can show as examples of their work; concern that there is a
  better use for these monies to address the cities basic needs; it seems

  JUSTICE FOR RENTERS ACT  16.C. Request of Mayor Davis and Councilmembers Torosis and
  Zwick that the City Council support the Justice for Renters Act.
  The California Secretary of State has verified that the Justice for
  Renters Act has qualified for the November 2024 state ballot. The
  Justice for Renters Action is an initiative which will expand local
  control over rent laws by replacing The Costa-Hawkins Rental

  12  October 10, 2023
 DocuSign Envelope ID: CA73D00B-DE18-430A-848E-969996FAF908

  Housing Act. Costa Hawkins prohibits rent control on single-
  family homes, condominiums and rental units that were built
  after 1995. The Justice for Renters Act removes this ban on rent
  control in California, giving local communities the right to
  stabilize rents and make apartments more affordable for low-
  income and middle-income renters. Repealing Costa Hawkins will
  help local government address one of the root causes of
  homelessness--skyrocketing rents and unaffordable housing.
  Mayor Davis and Councilmembers Torosis and Zwick also
  request that the City Manager issue a press release indicating the
  City Council’s support for the proposed ballot initiative and send
  a letter of support from the City to the Governor, Senator Ben
  Allen, Assemblymember Rick Zbur, and to the proponents of the
  Justice For Renters Act, was continued to the October 24, 2023,
  meeting.

  ENGINEERED  16.H. Request of Councilmember Brock that the City Attorney
  COUNTERTOPS  and City Manager consider developing and evaluate the impacts
  of an ordinance prohibiting the manufacture, sale, and/or
  installation of engineered countertops in Santa Monica. The
  fabrication of engineered countertops releases silica dust, and
  inhalation of silica dust can cause silicosis, a serious and deadly
  disease. On June 6, 2023, the Los Angeles County Board of
  Supervisors adopted a motion instructing the Director of Public
  Health to report on options to ban the sale, fabrication, and
  installation of silica fabricated stone in Los Angeles County. In
  addition, the California Division of Occupational Safety and
  Health has indicated that they will develop workplace standards
  for workers who handle engineered stone. Prior to developing a
  local ordinance, the City Attorney and City Manager are being
  asked to consider the findings of the Los Angeles County Director
  of Public health and standards developed by Cal/OSHA to
  determine its feasibility. - New item Received 10/5/2023, was
  continued to the October 24, 2023, meeting.
